questions.question: It's a city that sits on the eastern edge of the Honshu island, was once known as Edo, and became the seat of the Japanese emperor in 1868. Name the capital.
questions.explanation: Edo was renamed Tokyo, meaning 'eastern capital', when Emperor Meiji moved his court there from Kyoto.

questions.question: Sydney is bigger, Melbourne is more cultured, but the federal capital of Australia is a planned city tucked between them. Which city?
questions.explanation: Canberra was chosen as a compromise capital in 1908 to settle the Sydney-Melbourne rivalry.

questions.question: Rio de Janeiro had the beaches and the carnival, but in 1960 Brazil moved its capital to a brand new, purpose-built inland city. Which city?
questions.explanation: Brasilia, designed by Oscar Niemeyer and Lúcio Costa, was built to develop Brazil's interior.

questions.question: Toronto is the largest city in Canada, but the capital is a quieter place on the Ottawa River. Which city?
questions.explanation: Queen Victoria picked Ottawa as the capital in 1857 partly because it sat between English and French Canada.

questions.question: Auckland is the biggest city in New Zealand, but the capital sits at the southern tip of the North Island and is famously windy. Which city?
questions.explanation: Wellington became the capital in 1865 because of its central location between the two main islands.

questions.question: Nigeria moved its capital from the coastal megacity of Lagos to a planned city in the country's centre in 1991. Name the current capital.
questions.explanation: Abuja was built as a neutral capital between Nigeria's competing regions; Lagos remains the largest city.

questions.question: It runs north for nearly 6,650 km through Egypt and Sudan, and ancient civilisations rose on its banks. Name the river.
questions.explanation: The Nile is traditionally considered the longest river in the world, though the Amazon's length is sometimes disputed.

questions.question: It carries more water than any other river on Earth, draining a vast rainforest before emptying into the Atlantic. Which river?
questions.explanation: The Amazon discharges more water than the next seven largest rivers combined.

questions.question: It's the longest river in Asia, runs through Chongqing and Shanghai, and is home to the Three Gorges Dam. Name the river.
questions.explanation: The Yangtze is the third-longest river in the world after the Nile and Amazon.

questions.question: Born in Germany's Black Forest, it flows east through Vienna, Budapest, and Belgrade before emptying into the Black Sea. Name this river that touches ten countries.
questions.explanation: The Danube flows through or borders ten countries, more than any other river.

questions.question: At 8,849 metres, it is the highest point on Earth and sits on the border of Nepal and China. Name it.
questions.explanation: Tibetans call it Qomolangma; Nepalis call it Sagarmatha. It was first summited by Tenzing Norgay and Edmund Hillary in 1953.

questions.question: The second-highest mountain in the world has no romantic local name in common use, just a surveyor's code. Name it.
questions.explanation: K2 stands at 8,611 metres on the China-Pakistan border. The name comes from the Karakoram survey.

questions.question: It's the highest free-standing mountain in the world and the tallest in Africa, with a snowy summit just south of the equator in Tanzania. Name it.
questions.explanation: Kilimanjaro rises to 5,895 metres and is a dormant volcano with three cones.

questions.question: Symmetrical, snow-capped, and sacred to its country, this 3,776-metre volcano is the highest mountain in Japan. Name it.
questions.explanation: Mount Fuji last erupted in 1707 and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

questions.question: This vast desert stretches across North Africa from the Atlantic to the Red Sea, covering parts of more than ten countries. Name it.
questions.explanation: The Sahara is the largest hot desert in the world, roughly the size of the United States.

questions.question: It stretches across northern China and southern Mongolia, and gave its name to a desert horse and a famous Mongolian dish-of-sorts. Name the desert.
questions.explanation: The Gobi is famous for fossil discoveries, including the first confirmed dinosaur eggs.

questions.question: Lying in a strip along the Pacific coast of Chile, some weather stations here have never recorded a drop of rain. Name the driest non-polar desert on Earth.
questions.explanation: Parts of the Atacama receive less than 1 mm of rain per year on average.

questions.question: Mostly covered in ice but governed by Denmark, this is the world's largest island. Name it.
questions.explanation: Greenland is about three times the size of Texas; Australia is not counted as it is a continent.

questions.question: Off the southeast coast of Africa, this island nation is famous for lemurs found nowhere else. Name it.
questions.explanation: Madagascar is the world's fourth-largest island and broke away from the African mainland tens of millions of years ago.

questions.question: The world's third-largest island is divided between three countries: Indonesia, Malaysia, and Brunei. Name it.
questions.explanation: Borneo is home to ancient rainforests and the endangered orangutan.

questions.question: It looks like a lake on the map but is officially called a sea, and despite being landlocked it is the largest enclosed inland body of water on Earth. Name it.
questions.explanation: The Caspian is bordered by Russia, Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan, Iran, and Azerbaijan.

questions.question: It's the largest of the Great Lakes by surface area, sits between Canada and the United States, and its name simply tells you it's at the top. Name it.
questions.explanation: Lake Superior is the largest freshwater lake in the world by surface area.

questions.question: Its shores are the lowest point on dry land, more than 400 metres below sea level, and its waters are so salty you float effortlessly. Name this body of water.
questions.explanation: The Dead Sea sits between Israel, Jordan and the Palestinian territories at about 430 metres below sea level.

questions.question: Designed by Gustave Eiffel for the 1889 World's Fair, it was meant to be temporary. In which year was it completed?
questions.explanation: The Eiffel Tower was inaugurated on 31 March 1889. Many Parisians initially hated it.

questions.question: France gifted the United States a colossal copper statue, dedicated in 1886, that has stood in New York Harbor ever since. Name the statue.
questions.explanation: Designed by Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi with internal framework by Gustave Eiffel.

questions.question: Built more than 4,500 years ago as tombs for pharaohs, these are the only surviving wonder of the ancient world. Name and place them.
questions.explanation: The Great Pyramid of Khufu was the tallest man-made structure for nearly 3,800 years.

questions.question: Designed by Danish architect Jørn Utzon, with its famous shell-like roof, this landmark on Bennelong Point was opened by Queen Elizabeth II in 1973. Name it.
questions.explanation: Utzon resigned during construction and never saw the finished building.

questions.question: Carved into rose-red sandstone cliffs in what is now Jordan, it was the capital of the Nabataean kingdom. Name this ancient city.
questions.explanation: Petra was famously rediscovered for Europeans by Swiss explorer Johann Burckhardt in 1812.

questions.question: Perched high in the Peruvian Andes, this 15th-century Inca citadel was brought to world attention by Hiram Bingham in 1911. Name it.
questions.explanation: Machu Picchu sits at about 2,430 metres above sea level and was probably an estate of emperor Pachacuti.

questions.question: The smallest independent country in the world, both by area and population, sits inside the city of Rome. Name it.
questions.explanation: Vatican City covers about 0.49 square kilometres and was created by the Lateran Treaty of 1929.

questions.question: This tiny mountain kingdom in southern Africa is completely surrounded by a single other country: South Africa. Name it.
questions.explanation: Lesotho is one of only three countries entirely enclosed by another country, along with San Marino and Vatican City.

questions.question: It is the only country in the world named after a family — the dynasty that founded it in 1932. Name the country.
questions.explanation: The Kingdom takes its name from the House of Saud, founded by Muhammad bin Saud in the 18th century.

questions.question: He was the Macedonian king who, by the age of 30, had conquered an empire stretching from Greece to the edge of India. Name him.
questions.explanation: Alexander died in Babylon in 323 BC at just 32, and his empire fragmented soon after.

questions.question: The Athenian philosopher who never wrote a book, taught Plato, and was sentenced to death by drinking hemlock in 399 BC. Name him.
questions.explanation: Almost everything we know about Socrates comes from the writings of his student Plato.

questions.question: Julius Caesar was assassinated on a famous date in the Roman calendar in 44 BC. What is the date known as?
questions.explanation: Caesar was stabbed in the Senate on 15 March 44 BC, immortalised by Shakespeare's 'Beware the Ides of March'.

questions.question: In 49 BC, a Roman general defied the Senate by leading his army across a small river into Italy, triggering civil war. Name the river or the general.
questions.explanation: Caesar's words 'alea iacta est' (the die is cast) gave us the phrase 'crossing the Rubicon'.

questions.question: In 1215, English barons forced a king to sign a charter at Runnymede that limited royal power and became a foundation of constitutional law. Name the document.
questions.explanation: King John signed the Magna Carta under duress; it is often considered an ancestor of modern bills of rights.

questions.question: Between roughly 1347 and 1351, a pandemic killed perhaps a third of Europe's population. By what name is it usually known?
questions.explanation: The Black Death was caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, spread mainly by fleas on rats.

questions.question: This 13th-century Mongol leader built the largest contiguous land empire in history. Name him.
questions.explanation: Born Temujin around 1162, Genghis Khan was proclaimed leader of all the Mongols in 1206.

questions.question: This Venetian merchant claimed to have spent years at the court of Kublai Khan, and his book inspired Europe's fascination with the East. Name him.
questions.explanation: Polo's 'Travels', dictated to a fellow prisoner in Genoa, was one of the most influential travel books ever written.

questions.question: An Italian sailing for Spain, he made landfall in the Caribbean in 1492 thinking he had reached the Indies. Name him.
questions.explanation: Columbus made four voyages but never realised he had reached a continent unknown to Europeans.

questions.question: In May 1498, a Portuguese navigator dropped anchor near Calicut on the Malabar coast, opening a sea route from Europe to India. Name him.
questions.explanation: His voyage around the Cape of Good Hope began centuries of Portuguese trade with Asia.

questions.question: His expedition was the first to circumnavigate the globe, though he himself was killed in the Philippines before the journey ended. Name him.
questions.explanation: Magellan died in 1521; Juan Sebastián Elcano completed the circumnavigation in 1522.

questions.question: He painted the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel between 1508 and 1512, and sculpted David. Name this Renaissance master.
questions.explanation: Michelangelo worked largely alone on the ceiling, lying on his back on a scaffold for years.

questions.question: Painter, anatomist, engineer, and the man behind the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper. Name him.
questions.explanation: Leonardo embodied the Renaissance ideal of the 'universal man'.

questions.question: On 14 July 1789, a Parisian crowd stormed a royal fortress and prison, an event still celebrated as France's national day. Name the fortress.
questions.explanation: The storming of the Bastille has come to symbolise the start of the French Revolution.

questions.question: A Corsican-born artillery officer who crowned himself Emperor of the French in 1804 and was finally defeated at Waterloo in 1815. Name him.
questions.explanation: Napoleon was exiled twice — first to Elba, then permanently to Saint Helena after Waterloo.

questions.question: This Virginia planter commanded the Continental Army against the British and later became the first president of the United States. Name him.
questions.explanation: Washington famously stepped down after two terms, setting a precedent followed until FDR.

questions.question: In 1917, two revolutions in this country toppled the Tsar and brought the Bolsheviks to power under Lenin. Which country?
questions.explanation: The February Revolution ended the monarchy; the October Revolution brought the Bolsheviks to power.

questions.question: On 28 June 1914, the heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne was assassinated in a Bosnian city, triggering World War I. In which city?
questions.explanation: Archduke Franz Ferdinand and his wife Sophie were shot by Gavrilo Princip near the Latin Bridge.

questions.question: World War II in Europe began when one country invaded Poland on 1 September 1939. Which country invaded?
questions.explanation: Britain and France declared war on Germany two days later, on 3 September.

questions.question: Allied forces landed on the beaches of Normandy in the largest seaborne invasion in history. On what date?
questions.explanation: Five beaches were targeted: Utah, Omaha, Gold, Juno and Sword.

questions.question: On 6 August 1945, an American B-29 named the Enola Gay dropped an atomic bomb on a Japanese city. Which city?
questions.explanation: A second bomb was dropped three days later on Nagasaki, hastening Japan's surrender.

questions.question: On 9 November 1989, crowds began chipping away at a barrier that had divided a European city since 1961. Name the wall.
questions.explanation: The fall of the Wall was a key moment in the end of the Cold War; East and West Germany reunified in 1990.

questions.question: After 27 years in prison, this anti-apartheid leader walked free in 1990 and went on to become South Africa's first Black president in 1994. Name him.
questions.explanation: Mandela shared the 1993 Nobel Peace Prize with F. W. de Klerk.

questions.question: In August 1963, an American civil rights leader delivered the 'I Have a Dream' speech on the steps of the Lincoln Memorial. Name him.
questions.explanation: King drew explicitly on Gandhi's philosophy of non-violent resistance. He was assassinated in Memphis in 1968.

questions.question: This British Prime Minister led his country through World War II and is remembered for the line 'We shall fight on the beaches'. Name him.
questions.explanation: Churchill served as PM 1940-45 and again 1951-55, and won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1953.

questions.question: Britain's first woman Prime Minister, who led the Conservative Party from 1979 to 1990 and was nicknamed the 'Iron Lady'. Name her.
questions.explanation: The 'Iron Lady' nickname was given to her by a Soviet journalist in 1976.

questions.question: He was the Polish electrician who led the Solidarity trade union and later became president of post-communist Poland in 1990. Name him.
questions.explanation: Walesa won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1983 for his role in Solidarity's struggle.

questions.question: Elected in 1978, he was the first non-Italian pope in over 450 years and is credited with helping bring down communism in Eastern Europe. Name him.
questions.explanation: Born Karol Wojtyła in Poland, John Paul II served until his death in 2005.
